articles.title: The Doorway Test
articles.body:
A new sign above the community hall said, “Everyone welcome.” Inside, the committee had arranged a public discussion about the building. Yet one visitor could not enter through the main door without help. The sign expressed a good intention, but the entrance did not support it.

Before buying equipment, the committee invited people to try several everyday tasks. Could a parent enter with a stroller? Could a person using a wheelchair reach the meeting room? Could someone carrying shopping bags open the door? The aim was to notice practical difficulties rather than guess what other people needed.

The group used a tape to measure the entrance and the space beside it. They also checked the surface of the path. A loose mat created a small obstacle that had received little attention before. The distance from the gate was short, but the heavy door made the final part of the journey difficult.

Some changes were simple. The committee removed the loose mat safely and moved a table away from the entrance. Other changes required professional advice and a proper budget. Members wrote down which problems had been solved and which still needed work. They did not describe the whole building as accessible after fixing only one corner.

A clear notice showed an alternative entrance while further repairs were being planned. It included a contact number, but the committee understood that asking every visitor to telephone for help was not a complete long-term solution.

At the next meeting, the group discussed access as an ordinary part of how the hall worked. Welcoming people was not just about friendly words. It involved checking whether real people could arrive, enter, participate, and leave with as much independence as possible.

questions.prompt: What does the doorway test show?
choices: A welcoming message is enough on its own
Access should be checked through practical experiences
Only the inside of a building matters
Every improvement needs expensive equipment
questions.explanation: The committee learns from people attempting real tasks at the entrance.

questions.prompt: Which small obstacle does the group find?
choices: A loose mat on the path
A broken roof above the stage
A missing bus engine
A locked storage cupboard upstairs
questions.explanation: The loose mat is one of the problems noticed during the practical checks.

questions.prompt: Why does the committee avoid declaring the whole building accessible?
choices: It wants to stop holding public meetings
Solving one problem does not prove that every access need is met
Visitors no longer need to enter
The sign has been removed
questions.explanation: Several problems remain, so a broad claim would go beyond the work completed.

questions.prompt: What does “access” mean in the final discussion?
choices: The color of the sign
The ability to reach and use the building and its activities
The committee’s private address
The cost of buying a table
questions.explanation: Access concerns whether people can actually enter and participate.

articles.title: Why the Bus Average Was Not Enough
articles.body:
Five friends compared how long they had waited for the same bus. Four had waited five minutes each. The fifth, Rosa, had waited thirty minutes. When they added the waiting times and divided by five, the average was ten minutes. The calculation was correct, but Rosa felt that it did not tell the whole story.

An average turns several values into one useful number. It can make a comparison easier, especially when there are many records. However, it also removes some detail. In this example, nobody had actually waited ten minutes. Most had waited much less, and one person had waited much longer.

The friends decided to compare more than one kind of information. They kept the average, wrote down the shortest and longest waits, and listed how many journeys involved a long delay. The range of waiting times helped them see that the service was not equally predictable every day.

There was another reason to look beyond a single figure. A long wait did not have the same effect on every journey. Missing a casual visit was inconvenient. Missing a connection to a hospital appointment could have a more serious consequence. The passengers’ needs mattered alongside the measurements.

The group had only five records, so it could not describe the entire bus service fairly. It needed observations from different days and times. Rosa suggested collecting another week of information before writing to the transport office.

Their final note did not reject averages. It used them carefully. A useful summary can begin a discussion, but it should not prevent people from asking what the summary hides. Sometimes the most important part of a set of numbers is the difference between the experiences inside it.

questions.prompt: Why do the friends keep more than the average waiting time?
choices: The calculation is mathematically wrong
One number can hide important differences between journeys
Averages never provide useful information
Only Rosa’s waiting time should be recorded
questions.explanation: The correct average does not show how differently the five passengers experienced the service.

questions.prompt: What is the average of the five waiting times?
choices: Five minutes
Ten minutes
Thirty minutes
Fifty minutes
questions.explanation: The total is fifty minutes, divided by five records.

questions.prompt: Why collect records from another week?
choices: Five journeys may not represent the whole service
The first five records must be destroyed
Long waits stop mattering after a week
More records guarantee no future delays
questions.explanation: Different days and times may reveal patterns missing from the small first set.

questions.prompt: What does “range” help show in this article?
choices: The variety between the shortest and longest waits
The number of seats on a bus
The passengers’ ticket prices
The distance to the hospital
questions.explanation: Looking at the low and high values reveals variation hidden by the average.

articles.title: An Interview With a Repair Volunteer
articles.body:
This fictional interview follows Ben, a volunteer at a neighborhood repair event. Visitors bring small household items and learn what can safely be checked. The event does not promise to fix everything, and volunteers explain when a job needs a qualified professional.

Why did you join? “I wanted to share a practical skill. At first, I thought the work would mainly involve tools. Actually, listening is just as important. A customer might say a device is broken when the problem is a loose cable or an unfamiliar setting. We ask what happened before deciding what to do.”

What happens when someone arrives? “We write a short description together. Then we explain what we are able to inspect. The owner stays involved, so the event is not simply a free repair shop. People can learn how to notice a damaged part, find a model number, or describe a problem more clearly.”

Do you sometimes refuse a repair? “Yes. Safety matters more than looking successful. We do not open equipment we are not trained to handle. We also stop if a repair would create a risk that we cannot properly assess. Saying no honestly can be more helpful than making a confident promise.”

What do visitors learn from an item that cannot be fixed? “Sometimes they learn where to ask for professional advice or how to replace one suitable part instead of the whole product. Sometimes the answer is that the item has reached the end of its useful life. We discuss safe disposal rather than hiding that possibility.”

Ben says the event has changed how he shops. He now asks whether instructions and spare parts are available. For him, reuse begins before an object breaks: it starts with choosing something people can maintain and understand.

questions.prompt: What is the repair event’s wider purpose?
choices: To promise a repair for every item
To combine practical help, learning, and honest safety limits
To replace all professional technicians
To encourage visitors to buy more devices
questions.explanation: The event involves owners in learning and recognizes when work is outside the volunteers’ abilities.

questions.prompt: What does the owner do during an inspection?
choices: Always leaves immediately
Stays involved in the process
Signs away ownership
Buys a new device before any questions
questions.explanation: Ben explains that the owner remains involved rather than simply dropping off an item.

questions.prompt: Why does Ben value the availability of spare parts when shopping?
choices: It may make a product easier to maintain and keep using
It guarantees that the product will never break
Spare parts are always free
Instructions are no longer necessary
questions.explanation: His experience shows that future repair possibilities matter when choosing a product.

questions.prompt: What does “reuse” mean near the end of the interview?
choices: Continuing to use an existing item instead of discarding it
Making every item look new
Buying the same item twice
Ignoring all safety warnings
questions.explanation: Ben connects reuse with keeping products useful through care and repair.

articles.title: The Menu With Clear Ingredients
articles.body:
A customer asked the café staff whether a soup contained nuts. One worker thought it did not. Another remembered a sauce that might have been added earlier. Neither wanted to give the wrong answer, especially after the customer explained that she had a food allergy.

The manager did not ask the team to guess. She checked the recipe and the labels of the products used that morning. She also spoke with the cook about how the soup had been prepared. Knowing the usual recipe was useful, but it was not enough to confirm every detail about that particular batch.

The café then reviewed how it shared ingredient information. The menu used short descriptions such as “house sauce,” which sounded attractive but told customers very little. Staff created a separate list identifying the main ingredients and explaining whom to ask for further information. They checked the list whenever a supplier or recipe changed.

They also discussed the limits of the information. Removing one ingredient from a plate did not automatically make the whole preparation process suitable for every allergy. Shared equipment could matter too. The café avoided claiming that a meal was safe when the team could not establish the relevant facts.

For a customer, making a request should not require an argument. The manager encouraged workers to respond respectfully, ask clear questions, and seek reliable information. If the café could not answer adequately, it needed to say so rather than make a promise just to complete a sale.

The new list did not replace a conversation with the customer. It made that conversation more useful. Clear information, honest limits, and a willingness to check helped build trust. In this café, good service meant understanding when a simple-looking question deserved careful attention.

questions.prompt: What does the café improve after the question about soup?
choices: Its willingness to guess quickly
How it checks and communicates ingredient information and limits
The number of dishes it can call safe without checking
Its ability to avoid speaking with customers
questions.explanation: The café develops clearer records and more careful conversations.

questions.prompt: When do staff check their ingredient list again?
choices: Only after a year
Whenever a supplier or recipe changes
Only when the menu color changes
Only if a dish becomes more expensive
questions.explanation: Changes to supplies or recipes may change the relevant information.

questions.prompt: Why can “house sauce” be an unhelpful description?
choices: It may sound appealing without identifying what the sauce contains
It is always an incorrect name
It proves the sauce contains nuts
It prevents anyone from making a request
questions.explanation: An attractive label alone does not provide enough ingredient detail.

questions.prompt: What does “confirm” mean when staff examine the soup details?
choices: Make a confident guess
Check that the information is correct
Change the customer’s request
Remove all descriptions from the menu
questions.explanation: They consult the actual recipe, labels, and preparation information.

articles.title: Where Did the Puddle Go
articles.body:
After a rainy night, a puddle formed beside the school gate. By the afternoon, it was much smaller. One student said the Sun had “used up” the water. Another thought it had all gone into the ground. Their teacher suggested a better question: what different routes could the water have taken?

Water can leave a puddle in several ways. Some may flow toward a drain. Some may enter spaces in soil, if the surface allows it. Some liquid water may change into water vapor and mix with the air. That change is called evaporation. The water has not simply stopped existing because people can no longer see it.

The class began to observe the place more carefully after later rain. Part of the puddle lay on paving, while another part touched a patch of soil. Sunlight reached one side earlier than the other. Wind also changed from one day to the next. The students could not fairly explain every change using just one of those conditions.

They drew a simple cycle showing water moving between places and forms. The picture did not mean that each drop followed exactly the same journey at the same speed. It helped them connect familiar experiences: a wet shirt drying, a cold window becoming damp, and rain returning water to the ground.

The class used the word heat carefully too. A warmer surface can affect how quickly water evaporates, but looking at a disappearing puddle does not tell us exactly where all its water went. Different processes may happen together.

By the end of the discussion, the puddle had become an example of how ordinary observations can lead to scientific questions. The answer was more interesting than “the water disappeared.” It involved movement, changing conditions, and a willingness to look beyond what was immediately visible.

questions.prompt: What does the puddle discussion help students understand?
choices: Water can only leave a puddle by entering soil
An ordinary change can involve several connected processes
Sunlight makes water stop existing
Every puddle dries at exactly the same speed
questions.explanation: The article considers flow, soaking into soil, and evaporation together.

questions.prompt: What is evaporation in the article?
choices: Liquid water becoming vapor and entering the air
Water freezing beneath a gate
A drain filling with soil
Rain forming a new puddle
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains evaporation as a change from liquid water to vapor.

questions.prompt: Why can the class not explain every change with sunlight alone?
choices: Several conditions, including soil and wind, also differ
Sunlight never affects puddles
The students do not have notebooks
Water cannot move across paving
questions.explanation: Several conditions can influence what happens at the same time.

questions.prompt: What does “cycle” describe in the students’ drawing?
choices: A single measurement of puddle depth
A series of connected events that can repeat
The school’s morning timetable
A type of garden tool
questions.explanation: Their drawing connects repeated movement and changes in water’s form.

references.title: USGS Water Science School: the water cycle
